html:
The Lacandon, who call themselves Hach Winik ("true people"), are a small Maya people of the rainforest of eastern Chiapas, Mexico, near the Usumacinta River and the Guatemalan border. They speak a language close to Yucatec Maya.

Today's Lacandon descend mostly from Yucatec-speaking groups who moved into the forest in the 1600s and 1700s, out of reach of Spanish rule. An earlier Chol-speaking people, also called Lacandon, held the area until Spanish campaigns crushed them in the 1690s and moved the survivors away.

The modern Lacandon lived in scattered family groups, farming forest plots, and kept making incense offerings at old ruins of the Maya cities, such as Yaxchilan, into the 1900s. In 1946 Lacandon men showed an American visitor the painted Bonampak murals. Logging and new settlers cut their forest, the Lacandon Jungle, deeply after 1950. Their neighbours include the Tojolabal.
